extmeta.ImageDescription:
A Medieval ceramic floor tile (1350s-1390s). The square tile is decorated on the upper surface with a pattern in white slip and covered with a lead glaze. The pattern comprises a central quatrefoil within a lozenge border, at each corner of the lozenge there is a fleur-de-lys. A quatrefoil shape border encloses the pattern and there is a further fleur-de-lys in each corner of the tile. The tile is very worn with the majority of the glaze and sections of the slip decoration missing. The fabric is sandy with some clay inclusions. Jackie Keily notes it was probably manufactured in Penn, Buckinghamshire.

Dimensions: length: 110.60mm; width: 112.15mm; thickness: 21.51mm; weight: 383.32g.

Identification by Jackie Keily, Curator, Museum of London.

extmeta.ImageDescription:
A Medieval ceramic floor tile (13th – 14th century).  The square tile is decorated on the upper surface with a pattern in white slip and covered with a lead glaze.  The pattern comprises a central quatrefoil with a pellet between each foil.  Along each edge there is a semi-circle enclosing a floral motif of two petals and central stamen with a pellet to each side of the petals.  In each corner is a triangle pointing towards the centre of the tile.  This tile formed one element from a patterned pavement where adjacent tiles would have completed the semi-circular motifs to form circles with central floral patterns.  There are stray traces of glaze on the other surfaces from the firing process.  
Dimensions: length: 105.41mm; width: 102.96mm; thickness: 24.38mm; weight: 457.22g

extmeta.ImageDescription:
A Medieval ceramic glazed floor tile (AD1350-1400). The tile is decorated with a two-tone pattern comprising a central flower with eight petals within a circular border constructed from four strands with radiating ends which extend to the ends of the tile. There is a repeated pattern in between each of those radiating ends but the detail of the pattern is difficult to decipher.. The pattern appears to form part of a larger interlace pattern spanning several tiles. Some of the tile and the pattern are missing.

Jackie Keily suggests it was produced in Penn, Buckinghamshire. The fabric includes red iron oxide inclusions.

Dimensions: length: 109mm; width: 114mm; thickness: 21mm; weight: g.

Identification by Jackie Keily, Curator, Museum of London.

extmeta.ImageDescription:
A fragment of a line impressed ceramic floor tile, of later medieval dating (13th to 15th Centuries AD).

Approximately 40% of the tile is present and consists of a orangey red oxidised ceramic tile with a light brown transparent glaze with a line impressed design. The glaze extends down the original edges. The floor tile would probably have been triangular (corner) in shape. Three original edges survive, the central diagonal one indicates that the tile was originally made as a square and designed to be broken into two to create two triangular tiles.

The design present consists of three semi circles with a five petalled flower in the centre of the semi circles. The closest line to the flower appears to have part of a leaf and it spirals into the flower, suggesting it was meant to be the stem. The design would have been imprinted onto the wet tile using a wooden stamp.

The tile measures 96.92mm in length, 68.63mm in width and 22.83mm thick. It weighs 207.0 grams.
